one_liner: Header-only C++20 coroutine HTTP/1.1 server and client library. On the project's own plaintext test it beats nginx by about 3%.
what_it_does: cinatra is an HTTP/1.1 (and 1.0) server and client library that you embed in your own C++20 process. It covers HTTPS, WebSocket, chunked transfer, byte ranges, multipart, SSE, static files, rate limiting and a small reverse proxy with RR, WRR or random load balancing. You register handlers with `coro_http_server::set_http_handler<GET, POST>(path, fn, aspects...)`. A handler is either a plain function or an `async_simple::coro::Lazy<void>` coroutine, and routes can be exact paths, `:param` paths or regexes. It is a library with its own API, not a configurable server like nginx.
how_it_is_fast: The server runs one standalone-asio `io_context` per worker thread, with optional CPU pinning. One acceptor coroutine hands new sockets to those contexts in round-robin order. Each connection is a C++20 stackless coroutine, and a synchronous handler runs inline on that connection's IO thread, so the server never passes a request to another thread. Request heads are parsed by a vendored picohttpparser into `string_view`s held in a fixed array of 100 headers. The header scan has optional SIMD paths (SSE4.2 `PCMPESTRI`, AVX2, NEON) that you turn on at build time. Responses go out as one scatter-gather write or one string. The Date header comes from a per-thread string that is refreshed once per second. The responses to pipelined GET/HEAD requests are joined into a single `async_write`, and that helps a lot on pipelined plaintext tests.
when_to_use: You write a C++20 service that needs an HTTP/1.1 endpoint and client inside the process, and you want coroutine handlers without adding a separately built framework (header-only, dependencies vendored).
Small responses at high request rates over keep-alive connections, especially pipelined GETs. That is the shape of both the project's wrk run and TechEmpower plaintext.
You want WebSocket, SSE, chunked, range and multipart handling, plus a basic RR/WRR/random proxy, from one library.
Cross-platform C++ code: CI covers Linux (GCC 11.2, Clang 14), macOS (AppleClang 14) and Windows (MSVC 19.33).
when_not_to_use: You need HTTP/2 or HTTP/3. Only HTTP/1.x ships, and the HTTP/2 pull request (#748) was still open on 2026-09-26.

You want to replace nginx as a TLS terminator, reverse proxy or static-file server. Only a fixed-string response was benchmarked. The proxy supports only RR, WRR and random balancing, and the static directory is read at startup (new files need a restart).
You would switch from nginx for throughput alone. The measured gain is 3.4% from one self-run on a 4-core VM that also ran wrk, which is within typical run-to-run noise.

Your toolchain lacks C++20 coroutines (older than GCC 10.2, Clang 13 or VS 2022), or your project already uses yalantinglibs or iguana. The bundled iguana submodule causes duplicate-definition errors with yalantinglibs (issue #706).
Your handlers block, such as synchronous DB calls. A blocking handler holds up every connection on its IO thread unless you wrap the work in `coro_io::post`.

integration.dependencies: Standalone asio and async_simple, both vendored under include/. Optional: OpenSSL (CINATRA_ENABLE_SSL; the bundled CMake requires it on macOS), zlib (gzip), Brotli. The iguana git submodule is optional.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 with coroutines: GCC 10.2+, Clang 13+ or Visual Studio 2022 (per the README). GCC also needs -fcoroutines, and Release builds need -fno-tree-slp-vectorize.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows. Scalar parser by default. Optional SSE4.2 or AVX2 on x86-64, or NEON on aarch64, chosen with ENABLE_SIMD (only one at a time).
integration.thread_safety: Each connection and its handlers run on a single IO thread from the pool, so per-connection state needs no locks but shared application state does. sync_start, async_start and stop are commented 'only call once, not thread safe'. The server's connection table is protected by a mutex.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — cinatra is a library linked into your own binary. It does not read nginx configuration, speaks only HTTP/1.x, and its proxy supports only RR, WRR and random balancing.

gotchas: Pipelining works only for GET and HEAD. If a non-GET/HEAD request has more pipelined bytes behind it, the server replies 405 and discards the buffered remainder. Follow-on pipelined requests are matched only against exact routes, so `:param` and regex routes return 404 for them (coro_http_connection.hpp).

A handler registered on an exact path that throws produces a 503 whose body is `e.what()`, unless you install `set_error_handler`, so internal error text reaches clients by default. Handlers on `:param` and regex routes are called outside that try/catch.

GCC builds need -fcoroutines, plus -fno-tree-slp-vectorize in Release: build.cmake says SLP vectorization combined with coroutines causes a link error. The SSE4.2 parser path trips -Werror=array-bounds on GCC 13 (open issue #707).

Hash-flooding hardening is recent: #751, merged 2026-09-20, keys request-field maps with SipHash-2-4. Issue #752 is still open: when the application calls get_session(), a client-chosen CSESSIONID cookie becomes a key in the shared, mutex-guarded session map. The fix is PR #753, which was unmerged on 2026-09-26.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick cinatra over Drogon when you want a header-only library with coroutine handlers and an HTTP client in the same package. On throughput the two are close: cinatra led by about 14% in the project's own doc run (247,841 vs 216,982 req/s), and in TechEmpower's Round 23 continuous plaintext run (2025-01-30) cinatra reached about 14.8M req/s against Drogon's 14.7M. If beating nginx is the main goal, Sogou Workflow and H2O are in the catalog with larger claimed margins over nginx than cinatra's 3%.
verified_claims_summary: The project's doc reports wrk -t4 -c240 -d35s against GET /plaintext (13-byte body, same headers) on one 4-core 2.3 GHz Ubuntu cloud VM. CPU model not given; wrk ran on the same host over loopback. Builds used GCC 11 with -O3. Results: cinatra 247,841 req/s vs a tuned static-response nginx (return 200, reuseport, access_log off) at 239,629 req/s, about 3.4% more; Drogon 216,982; brpc 147,954 (on a different path). Separately, TechEmpower's Round 23 continuous run (Citrine, 2025-01-30, pipelined plaintext) had cinatra's best level at about 14.8M req/s (15.8M if a 15 s window is assumed), about 40th of 533 plaintext entries by my calculation from ph.json; TFB's nginx entry reached about 4.5M. At 16,384 connections cinatra logged 2,391 timeouts and 287 ms average latency.
status_note: Actively maintained: 1.0.0 released 2026-04-29, last commit 2026-09-20 (hash-flooding hardening), about 2.18k stars, 38 open issues. MIT-licensed and header-only with vendored dependencies, so it is easy to vendor, but it requires a C++20 coroutine toolchain.
